definition: Showing apparent knowledge of events before they happen.
example: The novel's prescient depiction of surveillance now feels familiar.
nuance: Prescient describes foresight; it does not require supernatural prediction.
options: Her prescient warning described the crisis months before it unfolded.
Her prescient warning merely recounted the crisis years afterward.
Prescient meant she could explain only past events.
Her warning was prescient because it was beautifully printed.
reasons: Accurate anticipation of a future event illustrates prescience.
Explaining only the past does not show anticipation.
Presentation quality does not establish foresight.

practice.prompt: Years ago, a librarian decided to scan all of the town's old newspapers.
options: The prescient newspapers had turned yellow and brittle in the damp basement.
Her prescient choice protected the records years before the basement flooded.
Her prescient choice came only after the flood had ruined most of the archive.
Prescient at every board meeting, she never missed a single vote on the budget.
reasons: Old, fragile paper suggests ancient, not foresighted; the word describes anticipation.
Acting long before an unexpected disaster shows foresight about what was coming.
Responding after the damage is a reaction, not an anticipation of the future.
This confuses the word with present; showing up says nothing about seeing ahead.
